title: Hercules
wpTitle: Hercules Reviews Round-up – Disney's new West End musical at the Theatre Royal Drury Lane

ratings.excerpt: The West End’s latest musical Hercules is a blast for the under 10s … This fun-filled adaption has retained the Disney animation’s goofy knockabout humour and refusal to take itself seriously … Disney stage adaptations tend to be conceived with a ruthless eye on the film’s pre-existing fanbase. Disney musical is fun, finely sung but not quite fit for the gods … Luke Brady is the hero navigating between godliness and humanness in a show that’s big on booming numbers yet short on emotion … ...  lightning does not strike twice with this stage version, although it is a sturdy enough Disney vehicle, with strong songs and plenty of splash. There is a briskness to its drama, under the direction of Casey Nicholaw, and a pounding out of the material – Songs! Lights! Action! – that makes it seem like a conveyor-belt musical. … ... the sound and optics are always eye-popping, the swivelling set designs intent on moving heaven and earth. Director/choreographer Casey Nicholaw’s production is pacy and family friendly, full of cheery songs and snarky jokes … ... Mighty muses save Disney’s musclebound musical … The new mega musical at Theatre Royal Drury Lane has new songs by Alan Menken — but why does it look like a Vegas theme park? … ... it’s hard to work up much enthusiasm about Casey Nicholaw’s musclebound production at Theatre Royal Drury Lane. True, the temperature rises whenever the five muses deliver hand-clapping gospel fervour — Zero to Hero still does the business — yet otherwise this is a show which ticks along competently enough. … The new numbers are efficient but unmemorable, nor is there much of a buzz about the romance between Luke Brady’s likeable hero and Mae Ann Jorolan’s winsome Meg. … The good news, though, is that Trevor Dion Nicholas adds mischief as Hercules’ sidekick Phil … Stephen Carlile makes an authentically sneering

Disney’s latest big budget musical is a fun spectacle with some great gags, but it won’t go down in legend … ... here comes Hercules, the next in the megacorp’s long line of perfectly adequate, not very imaginative adaptations of its bountiful ’90s animated roster. … Book of Mormon director Casey Nicholaw’s production is good looking and high energy. Robert Horn and Kwame Kwei-Armah’s book is appropriately big hearted with a handful of very funny gags. The show’s not-so-secret weapon is the retention of the film’s sassy quintet of singing Muses... Cheerful nonsense … Amiable Disney adaptation is shamelessly silly and flimsy … With its heroes and villains, its featherweight plot, its abundance of glittery numbers performed by a prancing, perma-smiling ensemble and its fantastical but relatively lo-tech mythological creatures, all served up with liberal lashings of camp, it has plenty in common with a big-budget panto. And it might be a treat for younger children or nostalgic lovers of the film, who squeal with delight at the recreation of each familiar moment. The rest of us are more likely to find ourselves craving a scintilla of nuance, a whiff of real jeopardy – any reason at all, really, to care about the antics on stage. … ... I love the original cartoon but Disney's Hercules musical fails to go the distance … Replacing Frozen as the Theatre Royal Drury Lane, Disney's Hercules bounces between divine and dreary but has two major things in its favour. … One of the greatest joys of the animated original was the sassy Muses. Their role has been wisely expanded, and these five swaggering powerhouse divas bring the entire auditorium alive time after time … All the brilliant big numbers from the cartoon are there, packed around the basic story … Alan Menken's melodies, of course, were sublime and, like the blissful play on words above, David Zippel's lyrics were packed with sly wit. Bursting with energy but lacking in heart … Hercules, the latest arrival, has all the qualities associated with the brand: it’s slick, it’s colourful, it’s energetic. It’s a show where it’s perfectly possible to have a good time. Yet something is missing. The wit and warmth that made the 1997 classic rather endearing have been replaced by something much more mechanical and heavy-handed. … The songs by Alan Menken and David Zippel supplement those in the film, but don’t ever produce a tune to touch “Zero to Hero … Hades himself (Stephen Carlile, doing his best) has been turned into a snarling pantomime villain, with strong echoes of Scar (who Carlile previously played on Broadway). Oh mighty Zeus! The Hercules musical is awful … I would recommend that you go quite some distance to avoid this … Great Zeus! What on Earth has Disney done to Greek myth and legend? This hideous grab-bag of classical mythology is based on the company’s 1997 animated film... Yet there is no escaping the fact that this new production, presumably intended for Broadway, is engaged in a continual, well, Herculean struggle with its own script. Robert Horn and Kwame Kwei-Armah have collaborated on a new book and the resulting two charm-free hours exist in a state of almost constant narrative bewilderment. … The Muses raise the tempo of Casey Nicholaw’s busy but unmemorable production every time they shimmy on in another set of eye-catching outfits, but aside from this it’s a dismal evening.

Musical lacks a punch in new take of Disney classic … ... he's been reduced from legendary hero to close to zero by a laboured new musical version of his derring-do, based on the 1997 animated Disney film. … Stephen Carlile adds spice as a Vincent Price-like Hades, and makes something of his panto-villain gags – including the groanworthy verdict on baby Hercules: 'So strong he could be a single mother.' … Pillars and statuary, shifting about in front of mosaic skyscapes designed by Dane Laffrey, add visual glitter. But the superhero action sequences are lugubriously undercharged, leaving Brady sleepwalking through adventures. … Music and lyrics by Alan Menken and David Zippel are audaciously bland. Like its demigod hero, Disney’s Hercules musical loses its divine status in clumsy hands … This show is lit up by sinuous harmonies and heart-melting ballads, but the warmth evaporates when the music stops … The film’s gloriously leftfield take on Ancient Greece... Unfortunately, there’s none of the same imaginative energy in this stodgy new stage version, which hits the expected beats without capturing the lovable zaniness that makes Hercules a fan fave. … ... even a dish of Angel Delight wouldn’t tremble at Stephen Carlile’s telly host-esque evocation of the ruler of the underworld … If the darkness is gone, thank the gods for star Luke Brady’s twinkly brightness as Hercules: he’s camp and joyful in a collection of truly bizarre Greek-style get-up... This musical is an ungodly mess. How did so many talented people get here? … Disney’s far from heroic Hercules fails to go the distance. Here’s how other shows got it right … Only the songs, by Alan Menken and David Zippel, have stayed constant — albeit the new ones are even less exciting than the ones they wrote for the original film. And yes, I know songs such as Go the Distance and Zero to Hero have their fans. But Menken, who has scored nine Disney films, has written many better melodies elsewhere. … Hercules staggers through its storytelling, going from the spectacular to the silly to po-faced balladeering.
